items.title: 12.9 Stability of the oxidation states of sulfur

source_refs.note: Topic 12.9 with Figure 12.9, printed pages 281-282. The original's Frost curves are schematic.

blocks.text: The stability of the oxidation states of sulfur is explained by a Frost diagram, a plot of nE standard against oxidation state n for the redox couple X(n)/X(0) (Figure 12.9). It shows the relative stabilities of the oxidation states at two extreme pH values, pH 0 and pH 14 (acidic and basic conditions). It can also be regarded as a plot of the standard reaction Gibbs free energy against oxidation state, because -delta G standard = nFE standard, or -delta G standard / F = nE standard, where E standard is the standard reduction potential, F the Faraday constant and n the number of electrons transferred. The more stable oxidation state has the lower nE value (more negative Gibbs energy), so it lies at the lowest position in the diagram; a couple with a more positive slope is a good oxidising agent, and one with a more negative slope a good reducing agent.

In the diagram for sulfur, +6 (sulfate) is the most thermodynamically stable oxidation state, completely non-oxidising under extremely basic conditions, while under extremely acidic conditions it is very unstable. In basic environments the oxidised sulfur states are all more stable than the elemental form, but under acidic conditions all the oxidised states are less stable than the element.

blocks.long_description: Sulfur bonds to itself with single bonds into crown-shaped eight-membered rings, which is why it is a yellow solid of low reactivity. Promoting electrons into its empty d orbitals lets it reach +4 in sulfur dioxide and +6 in sulfur trioxide and sulfate. On a Frost diagram the lowest point is the most stable state: in alkaline solution sulfate lies far below the element and is harmless, but in acid the oxidised states sit above elemental sulfur and are oxidising. Heated sulfur burns to sulfur dioxide, is oxidised by nitric acid to sulfuric acid, tarnishes silver and copper as sulfides, turns cyanide into thiocyanate and combines with fluorine to the inert gas SF6. Its uses run from vulcanising rubber through fertilisers and gunpowder to sulfa drugs, sulfur dyes and fragrances.
